title: Trump Gets the Owner's Box. Mamdani Bought Standing Room. Both Are at the Knicks Game Tonight.
excerpt: NYC's Indian-origin mayor — son of filmmaker Mira Nair, former rapper, Cuomo slayer — is hosting a rival watch party for 5,000 while the president sits in the suite.
body:
On Monday night, the most powerful man in America and the most unconventional mayor New York City has had in decades will both be at Madison Square Garden for Game 3 of the NBA Finals. They will not be sitting together.

President Donald Trump — a lifelong Knicks fan who grew up in Queens — is expected in a luxury suite alongside Knicks owner James Dolan, White House aides Steven Cheung and Dan Scavino, and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, his endorsed candidate for New York governor. Security at the Garden has been elevated to near-presidential levels, with a strict no-bag policy and fan areas around the arena shuttered by the NYPD and Secret Service.

Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani, meanwhile, will be nowhere near the suite. At a Monday press conference, Mamdani said he paid nearly $1,000 for a standing-room-only ticket. "I can tell you that I won't be courtside or in a suite, but I can't wait to see the game," he told 1010 Wins.

## The Indian-Origin Mayor Who Beat Andrew Cuomo

For the Indian diaspora, Mamdani's story is singular. Born in Kampala, Uganda, to Indian academic Mahmood Mamdani and acclaimed filmmaker Mira Nair — the director of *Monsoon Wedding* and *The Namesake* — he moved to New York at age seven after three years in Cape Town. His heritage is Indian, Ugandan, and South African all at once.

Before politics, Mamdani was a rapper performing as Young Cardamom, recording music videos in Uganda that namechecked his Indian roots. He worked as a housing counselor, ran campaigns for other candidates, and then stunned New York's political establishment by unseating a five-term incumbent to win a State Assembly seat in 2020.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZStoQ7EcPE/

In June 2025, he pulled off what many considered impossible: defeating former governor Andrew Cuomo in the Democratic mayoral primary. In November, he was elected the 112th mayor of New York City — the city's youngest in over a century, its first Asian American mayor, and its first Muslim mayor.

## Two Men, Two Americas, One Arena

The contrast at the Garden encapsulates something larger. Trump, the billionaire president who threatened to cut New York's federal funding if Mamdani won, will watch from the owner's box. Mamdani, the democratic socialist who has called Trump "a fascist" and signed executive orders to protect New Yorkers from immigration enforcement, will be in the nosebleeds.

Their one known meeting — at the White House in November 2025 — ended with Trump praising Mamdani, saying they "agree on a lot more than I would have thought." Mamdani's office has been cooler about the relationship since.

As the Knicks try to take a 3-0 series lead against the San Antonio Spurs in their first NBA Finals appearance in nearly three decades, Mamdani is hosting an alternative: a free official Knicks watch party at Bryant Park for 5,000 New Yorkers.

## Why the Diaspora Is Watching

Mamdani's rise resonates well beyond New York. In India, his mother's films are cultural touchstones. In Uganda, where his father was born, journalists who mentored him as a teenager speak of a young man who always asked how policies affected ordinary people. In South Africa, his old school has claimed him as an alumnus.

For Indian Americans, Mamdani's trajectory represents something new. He is not a tech CEO or a political appointee. He is an elected leader running one of the world's largest cities, doing it as an unapologetic progressive who embraces every strand of his multicultural identity — Indian, African, American — without hierarchy.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZVT7TWRK6V/

On Monday night, the Knicks will try to win at home. Trump will be in the owner's box. Mamdani will be in the cheap seats. And somewhere in the stands, as he has been since childhood, the son of Mira Nair will be cheering for the team he grew up with, in the city he now runs.
